trip.name: Sample Trip 2026
trip.notes: A worked example, not a real trip: eleven stops from Melbourne to Prague over three weeks, with flights, stays, a checklist, expenses and a full destination guide. Every name, address, booking reference and phone number is invented. Use it to see what a finished Jugni looks like before building your own.

checklist.task: Book the Helsinki to Tallinn ferry for the morning of 22 Sep - must land before the 15:25 flight
Register online for the Reichstag glass dome - free but advance registration only
Book Berlin TV Tower and the Spree river cruise
Confirm the Melbourne arrival date on XX108 - the ticket shows a time but not a date
Check passport has 6+ months validity past 29 Sep and 2 blank pages
Buy travel insurance covering Schengen and the Arctic leg
Tell the bank the travel dates and check foreign transaction fees
Buy a multi-country eSIM - the route crosses 9 countries
Pack thermal layers, gloves and a beanie for Abisko
Pack Type C/F plug adapters - everything except the UK-style outliers
Install an aurora forecast app before Abisko
Check what Chris needs at the Budapest car counter
checklist.note: Licence, credit card in the driver's name, and usually an international permit. Missing one means no car.

checklist.task: Sort a card that works in Sweden and Finland
checklist.note: Kiruna, Abisko and Helsinki are all pay-at-the-property, roughly SEK 4,745 and EUR 160 between them.

extras.title: The group splits 17-22 Sep
extras.content: Your tickets take you Oslo > Kiruna/Abisko > Helsinki > Tallinn > Budapest, and Chris has now booked the beds along it for the three of you - Kiruna, Abisko and Eurohostel Helsinki 20-22. Robin booked a different branch for the rest of the group: City Hostel Stockholm 17-19, Eurohostel Helsinki 19-21 and Premiere Classe Warsaw 21-23, all for 2 adults. Note both parties are at the Eurohostel on overlapping but different dates. Everyone reconverges at the Budapest apartment on the 22nd.

extras.title: Warsaw: considered, not booked
extras.content:
Premiere Classe Warsaw Airport - later booked by Robin for his branch
Sleep & Fly Warszawa
Hotel Gordon
All three were booking.com searches for 21-23 Sep. You fly Tallinn to Budapest on the 22nd, so Warsaw is not on your route.

extras.title: Oslo to Flam day trip - plan, not booked
extras.content:
06:00 depart Oslo, west on the E16
10:30 Laerdal Tunnel, 24.5 km, the longest road tunnel in the world
11:00 Stegastein viewpoint over the Aurlandsfjord
12:00 arrive Flam - lunch and the harbour
13:30-15:35 Flam Railway to Myrdal and back, past the Kjosfossen waterfall
15:45 drive back
20:30-21:30 back in Oslo
About 630 km and 14-15 hours all up. Car hire or the Bergen railway - not yet decided or booked.

extras.title: Worth paying for
extras.content:
Berlin TV Tower - observation deck, book online
Spree river cruise - the cheap way to see the government quarter
Reichstag dome is free but the registration is the ticket

extras.title: Budapest apartment is now non-refundable
extras.content: Free cancellation ran until 10 August 2026 23:59 property local time. That has passed, so the EUR 442 cancellation charge now applies. Booking.com paid AUD 70.67 of this booking, so a property invoice will not show that part.

extras.title: Helsinki to Tallinn ferry - two conflicting plans, neither booked
extras.content: One version of the spreadsheet says 07:30 arriving 09:30; another says 10:30 arriving 12:30. Your Wizz Air flight leaves Tallinn at 15:25, so the earlier sailing leaves a sensible buffer and the later one does not leave much. Nothing is booked either way - Tallink and Viking Line both run the route roughly every two hours.

extras.title: What to eat
extras.content:
Bratwurst: grilled sausage with mustard and a fresh roll
Pretzel (Brezel): soft baked, crisp crust, good with butter or beer
Currywurst: sliced sausage, curry ketchup, fries
Schnitzel: crisp breaded cutlet with potatoes or salad
Black Forest cake: chocolate sponge, cherries, cream

extras.title: What to eat
extras.content:
Smorrebrod: open-faced rye sandwiches with fish, meat or cheese
Frikadeller: pork meatballs with potatoes and gravy
Wienerbrod: the actual Danish pastry
Pickled herring: on rye, with onion and dill
Rodgrod med flode: summer berry dessert with cream

extras.title: What to eat
extras.content:
Atlantic salmon: grilled or smoked, and worth it here
Fjord trout: milder than salmon
Brunost: sweet caramel-like brown cheese, on bread or waffles
Reindeer steak: northern speciality, rich
Norwegian waffles: heart-shaped, with jam and sour cream

extras.title: What to eat
extras.content:
Swedish meatballs: cream gravy, mash, lingonberry
Gravlax: dill-cured salmon on rye
Kanelbulle: the cinnamon bun that fika is built around
Princess cake: sponge, cream, green marzipan
Toast Skagen: prawns, mayonnaise, dill, lemon

extras.content:

PIN 0000

extras.title: Pay on arrival, in local currency
extras.content:
Kiruna - SEK 1,595 at the desk, breakfast included
Abisko - SEK 3,150 at the desk
Helsinki Eurohostel - EUR 159.71 at the desk
None of these three are prepaid, so carry a card that works in Sweden and Finland. The AUD figures in the app are estimates at the 24 August rate, not what you will be charged.

extras.title: Two transfers, two parties
extras.content:
05:00 - ref 3000000001 - your car, ahead of XX106 at 07:30
07:15 - ref 3000000002 - two other guests, on a later flight
Both run Lina Apart to Istanbul Airport, about 10 minutes. The second one is not a duplicate and is not a mistake.

extras.title: Where to eat
extras.content:
Balık ekmek - grilled fish in bread - from the boats at Eminönü, eaten standing
Simit from any cart: the cheapest thing you will eat on this whole trip
A proper kahvaltı spread is a two-hour breakfast, so do it on the 10th, not the 11th
Karaköy for baklava; ask for şöbiyet if you want the one locals order
Lina Apart is out by the airport - eat in the city before you head back

extras.title: Free in one day
extras.content:
Blue Mosque - free, closed to visitors for 90 minutes at each prayer
Süleymaniye Mosque - free, and the terrace behind it is the best Golden Horn view
Spice Bazaar and Grand Bazaar - free to walk, haggling expected if you buy
Galata Bridge at dusk: fishermen above, fish restaurants below
The Bosphorus commuter ferry is a transit fare and beats every paid cruise

extras.title: Your one evening
extras.content: You land 11:40 and leave before dawn, so this is a single evening and a short night. Karaköy and Galata are walkable and lively; Istiklal Caddesi is busy until very late but touristy. A rooftop çay in Galata costs almost nothing and is the view people pay for elsewhere. Set two alarms - the 05:00 transfer is not generous.

extras.title: Where to eat
extras.content:
Currywurst at Konnopke's, under the U2 tracks at Eberswalder Straße
Döner: the queue at Mustafa's is 40 minutes, and any Kreuzberg Späti is 90% as good
Turkish market on Maybachufer, Tuesday and Friday afternoons
Sunday brunch is an institution - go before noon or book
Vietnamese in Prenzlauer Berg is Berlin's quiet speciality

extras.title: Free things
extras.content:
East Side Gallery - 1.3 km of painted Wall, open always, best before 10:00
Brandenburg Gate and the Holocaust Memorial - no ticket, allow an hour for both
Reichstag glass dome - free, but registration closes days ahead
Tempelhof: a decommissioned airport you can walk the runways of
Mauerpark flea market and its open-air karaoke, Sunday afternoons

extras.title: After dark
extras.content: Kreuzberg and Friedrichshain run latest; clubs rarely fill before 01:00 and the famous ones turn away more people than they let in. Door policy is real: small groups, sober queue, no photos, do not talk in the line. RAW-Gelände on Revaler Straße is the dense strip if you want options within a block. Sunday is a real club night here, not a wind-down.

extras.title: Berlin Art Week
extras.content: Usually mid-September - galleries and museums across the city open late with one ticket. The 2026 dates are not published yet; check before you go.

extras.title: Where to eat
extras.content:
Smørrebrød at Torvehallerne - order two, they are smaller than they look
A pølse from a street cart is the cheapest honest meal in the city
Reffen street-food yard on Refshaleøen - open through September, closes for winter
Bakeries: ask for kanelsnegle or cardamom snurrer, not a 'Danish'
Tap water is excellent and free everywhere - bottled water here is a tax on tourists

extras.title: Free things
extras.content:
Nyhavn, Christiania and Superkilen park - all free to walk
Assistens Cemetery: Kierkegaard and Hans Christian Andersen, and locals sunbathing
The harbour baths at Islands Brygge are free, and September is still swimmable
Many museums are free on the first Wednesday of the month
The Round Tower is cheap; the Church of Our Saviour spire is worth the fee

extras.title: After dark
extras.content: Nørrebro for the neighbourhood bars, Vesterbro for the busier ones, and Kødbyen - the old meatpacking district - for late. Beer is expensive enough that Danes pre-drink at home, and you can too. Bars stay open past 02:00 at weekends. Cycling home drunk is illegal and enforced here.

extras.title: Where to eat
extras.content:
Mathallen at Vulkan - the affordable way to eat well in the most expensive city here
Grünerløkka for cheaper kitchens and coffee that Norwegians take seriously
Shrimp or fish soup from the Aker Brygge quayside
Brunost, the brown cheese, is sweet and divides people - try it once
Supermarket dinners are a normal traveller move in Oslo, not a failure

extras.title: Free things
extras.content:
Vigeland Sculpture Park - 200 sculptures, always open, no ticket
Walk up the Opera House roof; it is designed to be walked on
Akershus Fortress grounds and the harbour promenade
Ekeberg sculpture park for the view back over the fjord
Allemannsretten - the right to roam - means the forests north of the city are yours

extras.title: After dark
extras.content:
Grünerløkka and Torggata hold most of the bars. Prices are the highest on this trip - a round can cost what dinner did in Berlin, so Norwegians drink at home first (vorspiel) and go out late.

Getting home: the metro runs to about 00:30 on weeknights, with night buses on Friday and Saturday.

extras.title: Free things
extras.content:
The aurora itself: no ticket, just darkness and a clear sky
Abisko National Park and the start of the Kungsleden trail
Kiruna's church, moved whole across town as the mine swallowed the old centre
The lake shore after dark, away from the station lights - the best viewing is free
Sunset over Lapporten, the U-shaped valley you cannot miss from Abisko

extras.title: Where to eat
extras.content:
Both STF stations serve dinner and it is usually the only hot option - book the sitting when you check in, not at 19:00
Breakfast is included at Kiruna, not at Abisko
Reindeer, Arctic char and cloudberry are the local plates worth ordering
Kiruna town has a supermarket; Abisko effectively does not - buy before you go

extras.title: The sky is the nightlife
extras.content:
There is no bar scene here and that is the point. Abisko sits in the rain shadow of the mountains, which is why it has the clearest skies in the Arctic.

Give your eyes a full twenty minutes to adjust, away from every light including your phone. The aurora often looks grey to the naked eye and green to a camera - that is normal, not a failure. Stay out longer than feels sensible; it comes in waves with quiet gaps between them.

extras.title: Aurora season
extras.content: Genuinely on while you are there. Mid-September is the start of the season: roughly 5-6 hours of proper darkness, and the lakes are still unfrozen enough to mirror it. Best odds between 21:00 and 02:00 on a clear night, looking north. Give your eyes twenty minutes to adjust and check the forecast each evening.

extras.title: Where to eat
extras.content:
Hakaniemi and the Old Market Hall - salmon soup, karjalanpiirakka
Weekday lunch buffets are the cheapest proper meal in Finland, roughly noon to 14:00
Korvapuusti - the cinnamon bun - with coffee, which Finns drink more of than anyone
Eurohostel has a kitchen and there is a supermarket nearby; use both
Tap water is famously good, so refill rather than buy

extras.title: Free things
extras.content:
Oodi central library - architecture, a terrace, and nobody minds you staying all day
Kamppi Chapel of Silence - free, and genuinely silent
Suomenlinna sea fortress - the island is free, only the ferry costs, on a normal HSL ticket
Esplanadi park and the harbour market
Temppeliaukio, the church blasted into rock, is cheap rather than free

extras.title: After dark
extras.content: Kallio is the cheap, lively quarter and is walking distance from Eurohostel. Punavuori for design bars, Kamppi for the busiest. Finnish bars run to 02:00 on weeknights and 04:00 at weekends. Alcohol above 5.5% is only sold in Alko shops, which shut at 18:00 on Saturday and all day Sunday - plan ahead or pay bar prices.

extras.title: Where to eat
extras.content:
Old Town cellars do black bread, elk soup and Estonian beer - touristy but good
Telliskivi Creative City has the better modern food and is 10 minutes from the ferry
Kohuke, a curd snack bar, is the thing every Estonian grew up on
Prices are noticeably below Helsinki, which is why the ferry is full of Finns

extras.title: Free in a few hours
extras.content:
The whole walled Old Town, UNESCO listed and free to walk
Kohtuotsa and Patkuli viewing platforms on Toompea hill - no ticket, the postcard view
Telliskivi Creative City: street art, yards, and the Balti Jaam market beside it
Ferry terminal to Toompea is about 25 minutes on foot, so the Old Town is walkable
St Olaf's church is free; the tower is not

extras.title: Where to eat
extras.content:
Great Market Hall - lángos upstairs, paprika and salami downstairs
Gulyás is a soup here; the stew you are thinking of is pörkölt
Ruin-bar food yards in District VII for cheap plates late
Kürtőskalács from a street oven, not a mall counter
Coffee houses in Pest are grand and cheaper than they look

extras.title: Free things
extras.content:
Fisherman's Bastion - the lower terraces are free, only the upper ones are ticketed
Shoes on the Danube memorial, and the promenade either side of it
St Stephen's Basilica - free entry, a donation expected
Margaret Island: a whole car-free island, free, good for the road-trip rest day
Walk across the Chain Bridge at night when it is lit

extras.title: After dark
extras.content:
The ruin bars of District VII are the reason people come. Szimpla Kert is the famous one and still worth it before 22:00, when it is a bar rather than a queue. Instant-Fogas is the biggest.

Széchenyi baths run late-night parties some weekends. Four nights here is the longest stop of the trip, so pace it - and always agree a taxi price or use Bolt.

extras.title: Budapest Wine Festival
extras.content: Usually early-to-mid September at Buda Castle, with the city spread out below. The 2026 dates are not published yet - check before counting on it.

extras.title: Free in a stopover
extras.content:
The Old Town is small enough to see properly in two hours and costs nothing
Čumil, the bronze sewer worker leaning out of the pavement - the photo everyone takes
The Blue Church (St Elisabeth) - free, ten minutes' walk from the centre
Castle grounds are free and give you the Danube view; the museum inside is not
Michael's Gate and the old walls, all within the same few streets

extras.title: Where to eat
extras.content:
Naschmarkt - walk past the first tourist stretch before you choose
A käsekrainer from a Würstelstand at midnight is a Vienna rite of passage
Coffee houses charge for the chair, not the coffee: one melange buys you an hour
Schnitzel done properly is veal and priced like it; pork is schnitzel 'vom Schwein'
Beisl - the neighbourhood pub-restaurant - is where the value is

extras.title: Free things
extras.content:
Ride the Ring on tram 1 or 2 for a normal fare and see half the grand architecture
St Stephen's Cathedral nave is free; the towers and catacombs are ticketed
Central Cemetery: Beethoven, Brahms, Schubert, Strauss - no charge
MuseumsQuartier courtyard - free to sit in, and in September everyone does
Prater park is free to walk; only the rides cost

extras.title: After dark
extras.content: One night only, arriving from Bratislava. The Bermuda Triangle near Schwedenplatz is the compact bar quarter and the easiest choice on a short stop. The far end of Naschmarkt runs later. Vienna's U-Bahn runs all night on Friday and Saturday.

extras.title: Where to eat
extras.content:
Walk one street back from Old Town Square and the price halves
Svíčková and goulash in a pub, not a restaurant with a menu in six languages
Beer is cheaper than water; ask for hladinka to get it poured properly
Trdelník is not Czech, whatever the sign outside says
Lunch menus (polední menu) are the cheapest real meal of the day

extras.title: Free things
extras.content:
Charles Bridge at 06:00 is empty - and you have a 06:00 departure anyway
Castle grounds free to walk; the buildings inside are ticketed
Petřín hill for the climb and the view, and the Lennon Wall on the way
Vyšehrad: the other castle, with almost none of the crowds
The astronomical clock show, hourly, free and briefly underwhelming - watch once

extras.title: After dark
extras.content:
Žižkov has the most pubs per head in the city and the fewest stag parties. Náplavka, the riverbank, runs late in good weather and is where Praguers go.

Last stop of the trip: the flight home is 09:15 and you leave for the airport at 06:00, so the final night has a hard edge on it. Trams run all night on numbered night routes if you misjudge it.

extras.title: Dvořák Prague festival
extras.content: Classical music across the city, traditionally through September. Dates and programme for 2026 are not out yet.

extras.title: Where to eat
extras.content:
Bryndzové halušky - potato dumplings with sheep cheese, the national dish
Slovak Pub on Obchodná for it done cheaply and well
You arrive from Budapest and leave for Vienna the same day, so this is one meal
Prices are noticeably below Vienna, an hour up the road

extras.title: Passing through
extras.content: This is a daytime stop between Budapest and Vienna, so there is no evening to plan. If the timing slips, the Old Town bars are all within the same few streets and the last train to Vienna runs late.

extras.title: Reffen street food
extras.content: The open-air food yard on Refshaleøen runs through the summer season and closes for winter around the end of September, so mid-September is one of the last chances. Check it is still open before crossing the water.

extras.title: Oslo Culture Night
extras.content: Kulturnatt - museums, galleries and venues across the city open late for one night, most of it free. Usually mid-September; the 2026 date is not published yet, so check whether it lands on your two nights.

extras.title: Helsinki Festival
extras.content: The city's big arts festival traditionally runs from late August into early September, so it may just have finished before you arrive on the 20th. Worth checking - the Huvila tent programme is the part worth catching.

extras.title: Vienna Design Week
extras.content: Usually opens in late September and runs into October, with installations spread across the city and most of them free to walk into. The 2026 dates are not out yet and you only have one night here, so check before counting on it.

extras.title: Check before you land
extras.content: You have 20 hours and no fixed plan, which is the perfect shape for whatever happens to be on. Istanbul's events calendar is worth a look the week before - a concert or a match will reshape traffic as well as your evening.

extras.title: Check the square
extras.content: Town Hall Square runs markets and small festivals through the warmer months, and September still counts. With four hours it is worth a glance at the calendar before you sail rather than after.

extras.title: Bath night
extras.content: Széchenyi runs late-night 'sparty' events on many Saturday nights through the year, and the baths themselves stay open late most days. Four nights here is the longest stop of the trip and this is the obvious one to book ahead.

extras.title: If you have the evening
extras.content: You have roughly four hours before the 15:25 flight, so this is a daytime visit rather than a night out. If plans slip, the Old Town bars around Town Hall Square run late and Telliskivi is where Estonians actually go.

extras.title: Check the Old Town
extras.content: Hlavné námestie runs markets and small events through the warmer months. You are here for a few hours between Budapest and Vienna, so a glance at the calendar the morning before is worth more than a plan.
